bullets.title: Honey Mama’s Mayan Spice Bar
bullets.note: Sometimes, it’s the small things. A few weeks ago, I found a secret stash of these in the fridge. When I raised an eyebrow, my girlfriend said, “You’ll be _very_ happy later that we have these.” She was 100% right. The taste and mouthfeel are otherworldly. More on Honey Mama: “We make each of our bars from five whole foods: raw honey, virgin coconut oil, cocoa powder, Himalayan pink salt, and either sprouted almonds or shredded coconut. That’s it!” If this bar sells out, all of their bars are ridiculous. **Please be a good neighbor and save some for others; I encourage you to buy** **no more than** **12 bars per household.** We all need tiny creature comforts to get through this, so please allow room for others.

bullets.title: Andy Goldsworthy: A Collaboration with Nature
bullets.note: This book was introduced to me under unusual circumstances that I’ll write about another time. For now, I can offer this context: I ordered it in response to a therapist saying to me, “I suggest you explore art, music, and so on. You know the problem with most books? TOO MANY WORDS!” If this exact book sells out, nearly all of Andy’s books are gorgeous, and [this trippy documentary](https://el2.fourhourmail.com/c/0vukl0mnnu9hg3094ho/rnt8hoheq0k2x6/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuYW1hem9uLmNvbS9SaXZlcnMtVGlkZXMtQW5keS1Hb2xkc3dvcnRoeS9kcC9CMDdHWVZSNUhMLw==) also does a good job of profiling his life and art. It’ll blow your mind.

bullets.title: Why coyotes and badgers hunt together
bullets.creator: Russell McLendon
bullets.note: fourhourmail.com/c/0vukl0mnnu9hg3094ho/7ps7h8hm0odk36/aHR0cHM6Ly90d2l0dGVyLmNvbS9ydXNzbWNsZW5kb24_bGFuZz1lbg==)). One paragraph to give you a taste: “Each member of the hunting party has a distinct set of skills. Coyotes are nimble and quick, so they excel at chasing prey across an open prairie. Badgers are slow and awkward runners by comparison, but they’re better diggers than coyotes are, having evolved to pursue small animals in underground burrow systems. So when they hunt prairie dogs or ground squirrels on their own, badgers usually dig them up, while coyotes chase and pounce. The rodents therefore use different strategies depending which predator is after them: They often escape a digging badger by leaving their burrows to flee aboveground, and evade coyotes by running to their burrows.” **I also highly recommend watching the following video:** [**Coyote and Badger Caught Playing on Camera**](https://el2.fourhourmail.com/c/0vukl0mnnu9hg3094ho/pdaeh9hl9zr385/aHR0cHM6Ly9vcGVuc3BhY2V0cnVzdC5vcmcvYmxvZy9jb3lvdGUtYW5kLWJhZGdlci8=)**. For some reason, I find this short clip so uplifting that I bookmarked it and often watch it when I’m feeling down or overwhelmed.**
